claims.text: Low-dimensional confinement in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons produces elevated interfacial and residual stresses.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons contain microstructural inhomogeneities arising from their constrained low-dimensional geometry.
Residual interfacial stress, dislocations, and defect clusters increase magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning suppresses and kinetically limits the magnetocaloric response of low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases magnetic hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Annealing at approximately 150°C for one hour in an inert atmosphere will relax residual stress in FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons.
The specified mild anneal can relax stress without significant grain growth or phase transformation.
Heat treatment can make a high-entropy transition-metal alloy magnetically more homogeneous by narrowing its distribution of exchange energies.
Mild annealing will partially homogenize the microstructure of FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons.
Annealing-induced stress relaxation and homogenization lower the energy barriers for domain-wall motion.
Reduced domain-wall pinning after annealing will decrease the magnetic hysteresis-loop area relative to the as-deposited control.
Reduced domain-wall pinning after annealing will increase the reversible magnetic entropy change relative to the as-deposited control.
Annealing will partially restore bulk-like magnetocaloric behavior in low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi.
The predicted improvement applies at magnetic fields below 0.1 T and temperatures near ambient.
Significant grain coarsening or phase changes at stronger annealing conditions may eliminate the predicted improvement.
The magnitude of hysteresis reduction and magnetocaloric enhancement depends on film thickness, initial stress, and microstructural uniformity.
Heat-transfer rate limits the allowable cycling frequency.

contradictions.description: The intervention is defined as an anneal that avoids phase transformation, and the boundary excludes stronger anneals that cause phase changes, yet the falsification rule treats an unintended phase change as falsification of the stress-relaxation mechanism. Such a phase change would instead mean that the specified intervention boundary was violated and would confound the mechanistic test.
